source_text: Bona ergo possibilitas mali atque boni voluntatem non cogit, sed permittit oboriri. Nemo igitur ideo bonus est, quia libero affectus arbitrio est; sunt quippe multi homines aeque liberi, sed tamen pessimi; sed nec ideo quisque malus est, quia liberi arbitrii est; sunt enim multi aeque libertatis huius participes, tamen optimi. Nec bonus igitur, nec malus homo ideo est, quia liber est; sed nec bonus, nec malus esse posset, nisi liber esset. Est ergo ista possibilitas, quae nomine libertatis ostenditur, ita a sapientissimo constituta Deo, ut sine ipsa non sit, quod per ipsam esse non cogitur. Contrariorum enim una capacitate ab utrorumque praeiudicio vindicatur; id est, nec malae voluntatis, nec bonae causa et necessitas dici potest, quae utramque sic recipit, ut neutram compellat existere. Necessariorum ergo singularis ductus, et unum quodam modo filum est, velut geometrica illa sine latitudine longitudo est, nec hic unio dividi potest. Quamdiu ergo singularis extenditur, vim naturae suae tenet; at ubi ei occurrerit quod in diversa findatur, illud necessarium illico terminatur. Id est, bonus Deus bonum fecit hominem.
pass_a_gloss: A good possibility of evil and of good therefore does not compel a will, but permits it to arise. No one therefore is good because he is endowed with a free decision; for there are many humans equally free, but nevertheless worst; but neither is anyone evil because he is of free decision; for there are many equally participants of this freedom, yet best. Neither therefore is a human good, nor evil, because he is free; but he could be neither good nor evil, unless he were free. This possibility therefore, which is shown by the name of freedom, was so constituted by a most wise God, that without it there is not what through it is not compelled to be. For by one capacity of contraries it is claimed from a prior judgment of both; that is, it can be called neither a cause and necessity of an evil will, nor of a good, which so receives each that it compels neither to exist. The singular leading of necessary things therefore, and it is in a certain way one thread, as that geometric length without breadth is, nor can this union be divided here. As long therefore as the singular is extended, it holds the force of its nature; but when that shall have met it which is split into diverse things, that necessary is immediately terminated. That is, a good God made a good human.

pass_b_english: The good capacity for evil and good therefore does not compel will to arise, but permits it. No one is good merely because he is endowed with free will: many people are equally free yet utterly evil. Nor is anyone evil because he has free will: many equally share this freedom yet are excellent. A human being is thus neither good nor evil because he is free, but could be neither good nor evil unless he were free. This capacity, indicated by the name freedom, was so established by the supremely wise God that without it there cannot be what is not compelled to exist through it. Its single capacity for opposites protects it from predetermination toward either. That is, it cannot be called the cause or necessity of either an evil or a good will, since it receives both without compelling either to exist. Necessary things therefore have a single course and, as it were, one thread: like geometry’s length without breadth. Its unity cannot be divided. As long as it extends singly, it retains the force of its own nature; but where it meets something divided toward different directions, that necessity immediately ends. That is: the good God made the human being good.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
